title: Neuroscience, the Natural Environment, and Building Design.
central_proposition: The human mind's split between genetically-structured neural systems and an internally-generated worldview leads to contradictory mental processes; contemporary architecture neglects the former, creating inhuman designs, necessitating biophilic design that incorporates natural geometry to reconnect humans and enhance wellbeing.

concept_definitions.name: genetically-structured neural systems
concept_definitions.definition: Part of the human mind that instinctively looks for information and reacts to environmental stimuli, shaped by evolution.

concept_definitions.name: internally-generated worldview
concept_definitions.definition: Part of the human mind that looks for meaning, giving rise to cultural, philosophical, and ideological constructs.

concept_definitions.name: biophilic design
concept_definitions.definition: A reconnection theory that incorporates organic life into the built environment in an essential manner, extending to building forms, articulations, and textures following the same geometry found in all living forms.

concept_definitions.name: inhuman buildings and cities
concept_definitions.definition: Designs created by contemporary architects that contradict physical and natural processes by imposing artificial meaning, failing to align with human biological needs.

concept_definitions.name: wellbeing
concept_definitions.definition: An overall sense of positive physical and mental state, enhanced by designs that connect humans to lived experience, with positive and therapeutic physiological consequences.

concept_definitions.name: human perceptual mechanisms
concept_definitions.definition: The evolved neural system that enables interaction with and adaptation to the environment, establishing our relationship and response to architecture.

concept_definitions.name: informational connectivity
concept_definitions.definition: The mechanism by which humans relate to biological forms and connect with the physical world, relying on information exchange.

concept_definitions.name: Biologically-based design
concept_definitions.definition: A design approach that utilizes observed effects and documents them into an empirical and tested body of knowledge, uncovering deeper causes for innate reactions to specific geometry of natural forms.

concept_definitions.name: Neurological nourishment
concept_definitions.definition: The positive physiological and emotional effects derived from engaging with environmental information and its organization, acting on all geometrical levels.

concept_definitions.name: Abstract human being (Level 1)
concept_definitions.definition: A conception of human beings as components placed into an abstract, mechanical world, interacting minimally and superficially with nature, disconnected and inert.

concept_definitions.name: Biological human being (Level 2)
concept_definitions.definition: A conception of human beings as organisms made of sensors, biologically connected (situatedness), evolved to perceive and react with inanimate matter and other organisms.

concept_definitions.name: Transcendent human being (Level 3)
concept_definitions.definition: A conception of human beings as spiritual beings connected to the universe in ways that transcend biological nature, enabling intellectual and creative achievements and a deep sense of self.

concept_definitions.name: Expert knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Complex environmental data that has become so internalized that perception seems almost extrasensory, forming a repertoire of patterns used to unconsciously match unfamiliar situations.

concept_definitions.name: Patterns
concept_definitions.definition: Schemata that identify certain preferred sensory inputs, control coordinated body movements, and generate the forms and connective complexity of traditional architecture and urbanism.

concept_definitions.name: Pattern Language (Alexander et al., 1977)
concept_definitions.definition: A codified framework of evolved patterns describing how humans interact with their environment and each other, providing a practical combinatoric framework for design.

argument_structure: The paper begins by positing a fundamental split in the human mind's processing of the environment, arguing that contemporary architecture has predominantly addressed only the 'internally-generated worldview' while neglecting 'genetically-structured neural systems.' It then introduces biophilic design as a necessary corrective, proposing that incorporating natural geometries into the built environment can reconnect humans and enhance wellbeing. The argument is structured around three 'levels' of human being (abstract, biological, transcendent) to explain the depth of human-environment connection. It draws on scientific research (neuroscience, environmental psychology, evolutionary biology) to establish the physiological and psychological mechanisms underlying these connections, particularly emphasizing fractal qualities, organized complexity, and symmetry. The paper critiques modern architecture's detachment from nature and advocates for design principles that align with human biological and evolutionary needs, culminating in practical design steps and a philosophical call for re-integrating science and spirituality in architecture.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism is 'informational connectivity,' where human neurological systems, evolved in response to the natural environment, process specific geometric and organizational patterns (e.g., fractals, hierarchical subsymmetries, organized complexity) found in nature and traditional architecture. This processing triggers physiological and emotional responses, including pleasure, stress reduction, and a sense of wellbeing. The absence of these 'neurologically-nourishing' patterns leads to prediction error, sensory deprivation, and negative affect. The connection can be implicit (physiological response without conscious recognition) or explicit, and extends to higher-level 'expert knowledge' patterns and even 'transcendent' experiences through higher-level neurological processes, which are seen as a manifestation of deep informational engagement.

findings.antecedent: Contemporary architects imposing an artificial meaning on the built environment
findings.consequent: Buildings and cities inhuman in their form, scale, and construction
findings.mechanism: Contradiction of physical and natural processes by neglecting genetically-structured neural systems, focusing only on internally-generated worldview.
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: By imposing an artificial meaning on the built environment, contemporary architects contradict physical and natural processes, and thus create buildings and cities that are inhuman in their form, scale, and construction.
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design (incorporating organic life, building forms/articulations/textures following living forms' geometry)
findings.consequent: Enhanced overall sense of wellbeing, positive and therapeutic consequences on physiology
findings.mechanism: Reconnecting human beings to the buildings and places they inhabit by aligning with genetically-structured neural systems.
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: Empirical evidence confirms that designs which connect humans to the lived experience enhance our overall sense of wellbeing, with positive and therapeutic consequences on physiology.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Empirical evidence confirms that designs which connect humans to the lived experience enhance our overall sense of wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Human perceptual mechanisms (evolved neural system in response to natural environment)
findings.consequent: Interaction with and adaptation to our environment, relationship and response to architecture and built environment
findings.mechanism: Instinctive craving for physical and biological connection to the world, rooted in human nature.
findings.source: 1. Introduction
findings.quote: The human perceptual mechanisms through which these processes work establish our relationship and response to both architecture and the built environment.
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Architectural forms and surfaces
findings.consequent: Emotional engagement with the built environment
findings.mechanism: Humans experience surroundings no differently than natural environments or other living creatures, relying on connection established via information exchange.
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design
findings.quote: We engage emotionally with the built environment through architectural forms and surfaces. We experience our surroundings no differently than we experience natural environments, other living creatures, and other human beings.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Recent investigations lead us inescapably to the fact that we engage emotionally with the built environment through architectural forms and surfaces.

findings.antecedent: Natural and built environments possessing intrinsic qualities (e.g., organized complexity, fractal qualities, symmetry, hierarchical subsymmetries)
findings.consequent: Strong connection, healing, sense of wellbeing
findings.mechanism: Neurological mechanism reacts to the information field (transmission component), inducing a physiological reaction (physiological component). Innate hunger for certain information types linked to brain's pleasure centers, controlling pain reduction.
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design
findings.quote: Both natural and built environments possess intrinsic qualities that enable such a strong connection, and which in turn can be healing. This works through the sense of wellbeing established and maintained in the life of those who engage with such a structure.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Some of the highest levels of sensory connection to the built environment have been evidenced in the great buildings and urban spaces of the past (Alexander, 2002-2005; Salingaros, 2005; 2006).

findings.antecedent: Fractal qualities in our environment (ordered details arranged in a nested scaling hierarchy)
findings.consequent: Positive contribution to human wellbeing
findings.mechanism: Innately 'hard-wired' reaction built into our neural system, not a conscious response to recognizing fractal patterns.
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design
findings.quote: A growing amount of research finds that fractal qualities in our environment (i.e., ordered details arranged in a nested scaling hierarchy) contribute positively to human wellbeing.
findings.empirical_support_cited: A growing amount of research finds that fractal qualities in our environment (i.e., ordered details arranged in a nested scaling hierarchy) contribute positively to human wellbeing (Hagerhall, Purcell & Taylor, 2004; Taylor, 2006; Taylor et. al., 2005).

findings.antecedent: Natural environments (including artificial environments mimicking geometrical qualities of natural environments)
findings.consequent: Faster hospital healing, pain relief
findings.mechanism: Specific types of informational input reduce pain, confirming a link between environment and physiological outcomes.
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design
findings.quote: Another direction of research has uncovered undisputed clinical advantages (faster hospital healing) of natural environments, including artificial environments mimicking geometrical qualities of natural environments.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Another direction of research has uncovered undisputed clinical advantages (faster hospital healing) of natural environments, including artificial environments mimicking geometrical qualities of natural environments (Frumkin, 2001; Ulrich, 1984; 2000). Pain relief in hospital settings is significantly improved by viewing natural (or videos of natural) environments (Tse et. al., 2002).

findings.antecedent: Neurologically-nourishing environment (visually complex, natural complexity, organized complexity)
findings.consequent: Physiological (emotional) reaction
findings.mechanism: Innately 'hard-wired' process, not conscious recognition; an innate information-processing system evolved along with physiology, acutely tuned to visual complexity.
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design
findings.quote: Reaction to a neurologically-nourishing environment is physiological (i.e. emotional) rather than intellectual. There is mounting evidence of an innate information-processing system that has evolved along with the rest of our physiology.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Yannick Joye (2006; 2007a; 2007b) reinforces our own conclusions on the essential “hard-wired" nature of the process. This is not the result of a conscious response to recognizing fractal or complex patterns in the environment: it is built into our neural system.

findings.antecedent: Ordered geometry of biological forms
findings.consequent: Healing effects on human beings
findings.mechanism: Underlying genetic factor; evolution has a direction towards increasing complexity, and all life forms share an informational kinship based on special geometrical complexity.
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design
findings.quote: We assume an underlying genetic factor as the basis for why the ordered geometry of biological forms connects with and leads to healing effects on human beings.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Many scientists now believe that evolution has a direction: the increasing complexity from emergent life forms in a primordial soup to human beings is not random (Conway-Morris, 2003).

findings.antecedent: Structures embodying organized complexity
findings.consequent: Stronger physiological and psychological connection in humans
findings.mechanism: The built environment performs a crucial function similar to the natural environment, influencing health and mental wellbeing through connection processes.
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment
findings.quote: Human beings connect physiologically and psychologically to structures embodying organized complexity more strongly than to environments that are either too plain, or which present disorganized complexity.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Human beings connect physiologically and psychologically to structures embodying organized complexity more strongly than to environments that are either too plain, or which present disorganized complexity (Salingaros, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design (intimate merging of artificial and natural structures, incorporating natural geometrical qualities into built forms)
findings.consequent: Reconnection of human beings to buildings/places, enhanced health and mental wellbeing
findings.mechanism: Human beings are biologically predisposed to require contact with natural forms and their complex geometry (Biophilia Hypothesis), just as they require nutrients and air.
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment
findings.quote: Biophilic design, as one of the most recent and viable reconnection theories, incorporates organic life into the built environment in an essential manner.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Following the arguments of Edward Wilson (1984), people are not capable of living a complete and healthy life detached from nature.

findings.antecedent: Artificial representation or substitute of nature (lacking requisite complexity, minimalist, monoculture)
findings.consequent: Poor human connection, underlying neurological disconnection
findings.mechanism: Fails to provide the complex geometry and informational richness humans are biologically predisposed to connect with, triggering neurological disconnection.
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment
findings.quote: This is a minimalist image lacking complexity and hierarchy. Biophilia demands a vastly more intense connection with plant and animal life, leading to the support of ecosystems and native plant species whenever possible.
findings.empirical_support_cited: While many architects may indeed claim to practice in this way, they more frequently replace nature by a very poor image of nature: an artificial representation or substitute that lacks the requisite complexity.

findings.antecedent: Buildings and urban structures incorporating essential geometrical qualities of nature (complex built geometry, organized details, hierarchical connections)
findings.consequent: Neurological nourishment, human connection
findings.mechanism: Engagement with information and its organization across all geometrical levels, from the microscopic to the city scale, provides neurological nourishment.
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment
findings.quote: Neurological nourishment depends upon an engagement with information and its organization. This connective mechanism acts on all geometrical levels, from the microscopic, through increasing physical scales up to the size of the city.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This belies a fundamental misconception about living structure, which connects on the human levels of scale through organized details and hierarchical connections (Alexander, 2002-2005; Salingaros, 2005; 2006).

findings.antecedent: Traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, shape of interior space
findings.consequent: Informational connectivity, direct neurophysiological trigger
findings.mechanism: Distillation of geometrical connective rules that directly trigger our neurophysiology, rather than merely copying natural forms.
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment
findings.quote: Traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, and the shape of interior space helped to achieve informational connectivity.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Long misinterpreted as a copy of natural forms, ornamentation in its deepest expressions is far more than that: it is a distillation of geometrical connective rules that trigger our neurophysiology directly.

findings.antecedent: Underlying geometrical complexity of living structure (expressed in biological organisms and artifacts/buildings)
findings.consequent: Neurological nourishment
findings.mechanism: Humans are nourished by this geometry, which is incorporated to varying degrees in living beings and human creations; the distinction between living and artificial is one of degree.
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment
findings.quote: We, on the other hand, believe that the underlying geometrical complexity of living structure is what nourishes humans.
findings.empirical_support_cited: We, on the other hand, believe that the underlying geometrical complexity of living structure is what nourishes humans. This geometry could be equally expressed in biological organisms as in artifacts and buildings: the difference is merely one of degree (Alexander, 2002-2005).

findings.antecedent: Traditional/sacred sites, buildings, and artifacts
findings.consequent: Intense human connection, healing
findings.mechanism: Informational content is successful in conception, connecting more directly to neurological processes, requiring less mental translation and interpretation, thus presenting itself as inspired or divine.
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment
findings.quote: The informational content in this type of structure is simply so successful in its conception that it connects more directly to neurological processes.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Not surprisingly, the most intense connection is achieved in historic sacred sites, buildings, and artifacts.

findings.antecedent: 20th-century architecture (formal, self-referential, autonomous, detached from nature)
findings.consequent: Separation from human comfort and shelter, non-responsive to human nature
findings.mechanism: Predicated on certain formal and abstract notions about space, materials, and form, neglecting human physiological and psychological response.
findings.source: 4. An architecture that arises from human nature
findings.quote: The desire to overcome nature, to separate man from the universe by placing him above natural constraints, led to the ultimate architectural assertion of the twentieth century, one expressing total autonomy.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This spectacularly beautiful work, elegant, formal, and totally detached from the world around it, represents a kind of counterrevolution in today's educational thought and practice." (Huxtable, 1999).

findings.antecedent: Architecture that considers human nature and neurological processes
findings.consequent: Healthier architecture, human sense of wellbeing
findings.mechanism: Aligning design with the tactile, perceptual, and mental processes necessary for human wellbeing, drawing from comprehensive architectural design methods.
findings.source: 4. An architecture that arises from human nature
findings.quote: To initiate this process towards a healthier architecture, we need to ask: what are the tactile, perceptual, and mental processes necessary for a human sense of wellbeing?
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Human beings as abstract, mechanical components (Level 1 conception)
findings.consequent: Minimal interaction with natural world, disconnected, sterile, non-interactive experience
findings.mechanism: This abstract conception of humanity, prevalent in contemporary thinking and architecture, represents humans as inert passengers, not biological entities.
findings.source: 5. Three different conceptions of being human
findings.quote: Here, human beings interact only minimally (superficially) with the natural world, a condition of being disconnected. This is an abstract conception of humanity, yet is representative of much of contemporary thinking.
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Human beings as biological organisms with sensors (Level 2 conception)
findings.consequent: Biological connectedness (situatedness), perception and reaction to inanimate matter and organisms
findings.mechanism: Possession of an evolved neural apparatus that enables receiving and using measurable input to make sense of the natural world.
findings.source: 5. Three different conceptions of being human
findings.quote: Here, humans are biological entities: animals that possess a sensory apparatus enabling them to receive and use measurable input. This is a condition of biological connectedness to the world, i.e. situatedness (Salingaros & Masden, 2006a).
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Human beings as spiritual beings connected to the universe (Level 3 conception)
findings.consequent: Transcendent engagement with the world, intellectual and creative achievements, deep sense of self
findings.mechanism: Connection through higher-level neurological processes, allowing for qualities that transcend biological nature and make possible intellectual/creative achievements.
findings.source: 5. Three different conceptions of being human
findings.quote: The third conception corresponds to the much older metaphysical picture of humans as spiritual beings, connected to the universe in ways that other animals are not.
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Industrialized, technological world
findings.consequent: Human beings become smaller, less significant components of a machine, biological/transcendental nature denied
findings.mechanism: The world is defined by machines and industrial materials, and information fields come from media images, suppressing connection to nature.
findings.source: 6. Level one: the abstract human being
findings.quote: Since this world has become an ever vaster and encompassing machine, so too its human inhabitant has become but an ever smaller (and, by implication, less significant) component of that machine.
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Visually sterile, industrial 'look' (polished metal, porcelain, sterile factory environments)
findings.consequent: Association with 'healthy,' suspicion of life forms, neurological disconnection
findings.mechanism: Misunderstanding that microbes can thrive on any surface, leading to a worldview where signs of life are threatening and nature is eliminated.
findings.source: 6. Level one: the abstract human being
findings.quote: A “healthy” environment became associated with a visually sterile, industrial "look" of polished metal or porcelain surfaces.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Early 20th-Century advances in microbiology and sanitary practices coincided with the introduction of industrial materials. A “healthy” environment became associated with a visually sterile, industrial "look" of polished metal or porcelain surfaces.

findings.antecedent: Human sensibilities detached from life forms, oriented towards artificial world of images/machines
findings.consequent: Insensitivity to healing effects of natural environments
findings.mechanism: Psychological conditioning to act against biological nature, making it difficult to explain the benefits of biophilic design.
findings.source: 6. Level one: the abstract human being
findings.quote: We are now facing a population whose sensibilities have been detached from most other life forms, and oriented principally towards an artificial world of images and machines.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This contemporary condition demonstrates that human beings can be psychologically conditioned to act against their biological nature (Hoffer, 1951; Salingaros, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Built environment that is neurologically non-nourishing
findings.consequent: Negative physiological and psychological reaction (anxiety, distress)
findings.mechanism: Human genetic structure and neurophysiologic requirements remain constant over millennia, leading to instinctive negative responses to environments lacking evolved sensory inputs.
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being
findings.quote: Therefore, we will instinctively react in a negative manner to a built environment that is neurologically non-nourishing, or which might actually cause physical anxiety and distress.
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Geometry of the environment (in hospital design)
findings.consequent: Patient healing time
findings.mechanism: Specific environmental features (e.g., natural views) reduce stress and promote recovery, as shown by pioneering work in this topic.
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being
findings.quote: In hospital design, the geometry of the environment plays a significant role in how long it takes for a patient to be cured.
findings.empirical_support_cited: In hospital design, the geometry of the environment plays a significant role in how long it takes for a patient to be cured. Roger Ulrich has done pioneering work in this topic (Ulrich, 1984; 2000).

findings.antecedent: Environments deliberately eschewing natural visual elements (detail, contrast, symmetries, connections)
findings.consequent: Negative consequences for physiology, mental health, and wellbeing
findings.mechanism: The eye/brain system evolved to perceive and engage with these features; their absence creates neurological non-nourishment.
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being
findings.quote: Creating an environment that deliberately eschews these elements (visual elements which are found in nature and in all traditional architectures) has negative consequences for our physiology, and thus for our mental health and sense of wellbeing.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Our eye/brain system has evolved to perceive fine detail, contrast, symmetries, color, and connections.

findings.antecedent: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information (colorless, drab, minimalist surfaces/spaces)
findings.consequent: Mimic signs of human pathology (macular degeneration, stroke, cerebral achromatopsia, visual agnosia), anxiety
findings.mechanism: Lack of visual complexity and information creates a sensation similar to sensory deprivation and neurophysiologic breakdown.
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being
findings.quote: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information mimic signs of human pathology.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information mimic signs of human pathology. For example, colorless, drab, minimalist surfaces and spaces reproduce clinical symptoms of macular degeneration, stroke, cerebral achromatopsia, and visual agnosia (Salingaros, 2003; 2006).

findings.antecedent: Naturalistic and stimulating habitats (for zoo animals)
findings.consequent: Improved psychological and social well-being, normal/healthier behavior patterns
findings.mechanism: Provides requisite environmental complexity and stimulation that animals are biologically adapted to, reversing neurotic and antisocial behaviors observed in drab environments.
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being
findings.quote: Moved to more naturalistic and stimulating habitats, the animals returned to more normal, healthier behavior patterns.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Judith Heerwagen has studied zoo animal behavior in naturalistic versus more artificial environments (Heerwagen, 2005). Starting from substantial observations of zoo animals, she reports the results of implementing a transformation towards more naturalistic habitats. As a consequence, the animals' psychological and social well-being has been drastically improved.

findings.antecedent: Information-rich environments (for young rats)
findings.consequent: Increased brain size, improved neural connectivity (up to 20%), better intelligence test performance
findings.mechanism: Fulfillment of a necessary external component in the brain's development, optimizing cortical physiology responsible for intelligence.
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being
findings.quote: Evidence has been accumulating since the 1960s that complexity and stimulation in the environment can lead to increased intelligence of a developing animal.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Evidence has been accumulating since the 1960s that complexity and stimulation in the environment can lead to increased intelligence of a developing animal. Incontrovertible results are obtained with young rats raised in information-rich environments, whose brains increase in size, and can improve their neural connectivity by up to 20% (Squire & Kandel, 1999: page 200).

findings.antecedent: Room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail
findings.consequent: Marked physiological response in favor
findings.mechanism: Physiological effects of the environment cannot always be consciously recognized, indicating an implicit, automatic response.
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being
findings.quote: physiological monitors recorded a marked response in favor of the room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail (Tsunetsugu, Miyazaki & Sato, 2005). We (and the study's authors) conclude that physiological effects of the environment cannot always be consciously recognized.
findings.empirical_support_cited: physiological monitors recorded a marked response in favor of the room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail (Tsunetsugu, Miyazaki & Sato, 2005).

findings.antecedent: Complex environmental data internalized ('expert knowledge')
findings.consequent: Perception seems extrasensory, unconscious matching of unfamiliar situations, well-developed perceptual skills
findings.mechanism: Learning shapes neural networks after birth, acquiring non-genetic properties like structural and functional pattern recognition, which work as a seamless whole with genetic components.
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns
findings.quote: Experience represents a sensory response that has become too complex for us to easily describe, categorize, or understand in an analytic manner. Experience provides us with a repertoire of patterns, which we then use to unconsciously match unfamiliar situations (Klein, 1998).
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Emotional learning (from sensory input)
findings.consequent: Subconscious storage (nondeclarative memory), positive emotion
findings.mechanism: Works independently of conscious memory, evoking positive emotion because it satisfies an innate internal template that evolved with our behavior.
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns
findings.quote: Emotional learning is the result of sensory input, but remains subconscious (i.e. stored in nondeclarative memory).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Emotional learning is the result of sensory input, but remains subconscious (i.e. stored in nondeclarative memory). It works independently of conscious (declarative) memory, since much of the information that we process is not accessible to conscious awareness (Squire & Kandel, 1999).

findings.antecedent: Patterns (in human activity, speech, behavior)
findings.consequent: Organization of individual actions into complex wholes, generation of forms/connective complexity in traditional architecture/urbanism
findings.mechanism: Schemata identify preferred sensory inputs and control coordinated body movements, leading to the complex forms and connectivity observed in traditional built environments.
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns
findings.quote: Almost every human activity will be found to contain patterns, and those patterns generate the forms and connective complexity of traditional architecture and urbanism (Alexander et. al., 1977).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cognitive psychologists recognize patterns as schemata that identify certain preferred sensory inputs. Patterns also control coordinated body movements.

findings.antecedent: Alexander's Pattern Language
findings.consequent: Codified evolved patterns of human-environment interaction, practical combinatoric framework for design, anticipation/support of biophilic design
findings.mechanism: Patterns represent evolved solutions for human needs, combining social and geometrical elements, which were rediscovered repeatedly by traditional societies.
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns
findings.quote: Christopher Alexander's Pattern Language codified evolved patterns of how humans interact with their environment and with each other.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Christopher Alexander's Pattern Language codified evolved patterns of how humans interact with their environment and with each other (Alexander et. al., 1977).

findings.antecedent: Evolutionary convergence
findings.consequent: Small number of adaptive architectural and urban patterns arising spontaneously across cultures/times
findings.mechanism: Evolution repeatedly finds a relatively small number of working prototypes from a vast solution space, characterized by morphological similarity, by exploring adaptive possibilities.
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns
findings.quote: In the same way, a small number of architectural and urban patterns combining social and geometrical elements have arisen spontaneously in different cultures and in different times.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Today, we understand evolutionary convergence as a fundamental indicator of the parallel, independent evolution of specific patterns (Conway-Morris, 2003).

findings.antecedent: Systems mimicking human patterns of speech, movement, behavior (e.g., ELIZA, Brooks' robots)
findings.consequent: Emulation of human qualities/emotions, engagement of observers
findings.mechanism: Observer interacts through patterns of specific complexity characteristic of living and human beings, which are detected by sensory apparatus.
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions
findings.quote: As the above examples make clear, it is possible to emulate human qualities and emotions, at least partially, by means of programs that mimic patterns of speech, movement, and behavior.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Alan Turing (1950) devised the oldest test meant to distinguish a human being from inanimate information processors (i.e. computers).

findings.antecedent: Human-animal interactions (contact with domestic animals)
findings.consequent: Positive emotional and health effects
findings.mechanism: Information exchange via richly complex, pattern-based information, which is a key aspect of human connection to non-human systems.
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions
findings.quote: In recent years, more rigorous evidence has been accumulating on the therapeutic effects of animal contact (Barker, 1999).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Since the beginnings of history, people have benefited from (and documented) the positive emotional and health effects of contact with domestic animals.

findings.antecedent: Complex, organized informational patterns (evolved with human body)
findings.consequent: Recognizable humanity, sensory apparatus detects kinship of perceived patterns to self
findings.mechanism: These patterns constitute what makes us recognizably human and allow our sensory apparatus to instantly detect their degree of kinship to our own selves.
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions
findings.quote: What makes us recognizably human is a set of complex, organized informational patterns that evolved along with our body. Our sensory apparatus instantly detects the degree of kinship of any perceived patterns to our own selves.
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Abstract forms of architecture (lacking complex, organized informational patterns)
findings.consequent: Detachment from the perceivable world
findings.mechanism: Neurological hardware requires a far greater degree of information than the abstract forms of architecture currently provide, resulting in informational coding being missing.
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions
findings.quote: The processes at work in our neurological hardware require a far greater degree of information than the abstract forms of architecture currently provide. Informational coding is missing from today's architecture.
findings.empirical_support_cited: null

findings.antecedent: Twentieth century (technological progress, abstract ideology)

findings.antecedent: Buildings with intense degree of connection (e.g., sacred sites, traditional architecture)

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design (recognizing human-environment connections, coherent information, multiple levels of complexity)
findings.consequent: Re-orientation of architecture towards human wellbeing and emotional nourishment

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Designs that incorporate microstructure of natural materials or fine-grained texture/ornament, immediately accessible to human contact, will elicit stronger positive physiological responses than designs lacking such detail.

Buildings designed with a definite scaling hierarchy, where elements on successive scales maintain a ratio between 2 and 5 (ideally ~3), and no scale is missing, will enhance human wellbeing more than designs with distorted or missing scales.

Architectural designs featuring richness of subsymmetries on smaller and intermediate scales, acting throughout a scaling hierarchy, will lead to greater visual coherence and positive human response than designs with only overall symmetry or repeated identical components.

Small-scale construction systems that preserve natural materials for visible surfaces in human-accessible regions will optimize informational load and elicit more pleasurable feedback than systems that hide materials with high informational content.

Large-scale construction utilizing modular production of ornamental panels and building components that extend neurologically-engaging patterns (e.g., Islamic tiling, Guimard, Sullivan, Wright styles) will contribute positively to human wellbeing.

Re-using natural materials from older buildings (e.g., salvage yards) that establish scaling hierarchy and high informational content will result in more neurologically nourishing environments than using new, undifferentiated materials.
Concrete surfaces at human level, molded with patterns or incorporating permanent aggregate, will provide more positive sensory feedback than random textured or unfriendly flat concrete panels.

Allowing workmen freedom for individual expression in construction (e.g., laying tiles, adjusting window dimensions) will foster more pleasurable feedback and imbue architecture with 'life' compared to rigidly controlled, frozen designs.

High technology, such as robotic manufacturing programmed to emulate variations in material placement, can create individual building components with a degree of 'life' similar to hand-made crafts, leading to enhanced human connection.

A small proportion of custom work and custom-made components, or standard materials whose dimensions fit a biologically-structured fractal scaling scheme, can provide significant neurological connection and wellbeing.

Geometrical interweaving of plant life and natural features with building fabric, meandering/crenellated boundaries, and complex nature at an intimate scale (1-2 meters) within rooms will enhance biophilic connection and wellbeing.

Focusing intelligence and technology on creating and reinforcing natural geometry where it is absent or existing, and allowing natural geometry/life (weathering, plants) on buildings, will lead to more viscerally responsive environments.

Urban geometries that permit pedestrian access to and interaction with accessible, coherently designed gardens and natural spaces (breaking up suburban 'no-man's-land') will enhance human-nature connection and wellbeing.

Broader urban planning that avoids uniformity, designs complex natural areas, resists amalgamation into single 'parks,' and promotes a natural (fractal) distribution of green space sizes will better support visual and biological complexity and human wellbeing.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly links its findings to Christopher Alexander's Pattern Language (Alexander et. al., 1977), stating that the patterns anticipate and support biophilic design and make sense 'ONLY within the context of biophilic design.'

It connects the concept of 'expert knowledge' to the idea of patterns, where complex environmental data becomes internalized and used to unconsciously match unfamiliar situations, aligning with cognitive psychology's schemata.

The discussion of human-machine and human-animal interactions (Turing Test, ELIZA, Brooks' robots, pet therapy) serves as a warrant for the human need and capacity for information exchange, suggesting analogous mechanisms for architectural connection.

The paper draws on Edward Wilson's Biophilia Hypothesis (Wilson, 1984; Kellert & Wilson, 1993) as a foundational argument for the human biological predisposition to require contact with natural forms and complex geometry.
It references Stress Recovery Theory (Ulrich, 1984; 2000) by citing clinical advantages of natural environments for faster hospital healing and pain relief.
The paper connects fractal patterns in architecture to the brain's neural organization (Goldberger, 1996), suggesting a deep, non-coincidental parallel.

It links the concept of 'transcendence' to higher-level neurological processes and the 'animating aspect of self,' drawing parallels with philosophical and religious understandings of human connection to the universe.
methodological_critiques: The paper critiques architectural academia for neglecting human physiological and psychological responses to the built environment, despite decades of experimental findings, instead seeking 'greater distance and obscurity in the ethereal terrain of contemporary philosophies.'

It criticizes the reliance on surveys for measuring user preferences, noting that earlier studies showing only moderate preferences might reflect 'conditioned response,' and advocates for clinical studies using physiological monitors which can reveal preferences even when consciously unrecognized.

The paper implicitly critiques modern architectural practices for replacing genuine nature with 'poor images of nature' (artificial representations, minimalist lawns, monocultures) that lack requisite complexity and fail to provide neurological nourishment.

It critiques the 20th-century architectural trend of 'total autonomy' and 'separation from nature,' which led to 'ill-fitting, over-exaggerated, and often idiosyncratic formal architectural schemes' that impose design against human instincts.
model_structure: The paper proposes a multi-layered model of human-environment interaction, starting with a fundamental split in the human mind (genetically-structured neural systems vs. internally-generated worldview). It then outlines three 'levels' of human being (abstract, biological, transcendent) that correspond to varying degrees of connection to the environment. The core mechanism is 'informational connectivity,' where specific geometric and organizational patterns in the environment (fractals, symmetry, hierarchy) are processed by evolved neural systems, leading to physiological and psychological outcomes (wellbeing, healing, emotional response). This model integrates biological predisposition (Biophilia), stress recovery, and cognitive processing (pattern recognition, implicit evaluation) to explain how the built environment can provide 'neurological nourishment' and even 'transcendence' when it aligns with these innate human needs.
limitations: The paper acknowledges that the full mechanism by which certain environmental effects act on human beings (especially those related to 'mystery' and 'transcendence') is not yet fully understood and may not be entirely open to human comprehension.

It notes a practical limitation for the 'mathematical/sacred' method of biophilic design compared to the 'high-tech' method, as the latter is 'already in line with the industrial building/economic engine of our global society,' implying greater ease of implementation for the high-tech approach.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, which is crucial for their health and well-being.
Exposure to natural environments can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue, improving cognitive function.
Viewing natural scenes can lead to physiological and psychological stress reduction, promoting relaxation and recovery.
A design approach that intentionally incorporates natural elements and processes into the built environment to foster human connection with nature and enhance well-being.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper describes a causal mechanism where the integration of natural elements in building design influences human physiological and psychological states, leading to improved well-being and cognitive function.

steps.from_construct: Presence of natural elements in built environment (e.g., views of nature, natural light, natural patterns)

steps.to_construct: Reduced sympathetic nervous system activity / Increased parasympathetic activity
Improved mood, cognitive performance, and overall well-being
